events.text: Your cradle is a drift of cloud that a minor ministry is paid to keep dry. Nine tutors queue at the door before dawn, ranked by how deeply the Court bows to them. You are very small, and you have already noticed that every grown immortal arranges their face before they come in.

effects.log: You pull the lead tutor's beard with great determination. The nine bow lower afterwards, and one of them, privately, is delighted.
You hide under the cloud-quilt until the tutors give up and take tea. It is your first lesson in how much the Court will wait for you.
You greet each tutor by title, in order, as you were not taught. The ministry that keeps your cloud dry puts it in a report.

events.text: Your first lesson is the white jade stairs, and who stands on which step. You are given the ninth from the top, which is absurdly high, and told never to stand lower, even if someone older asks. A very old marshal climbs up to ask whether you understand. Behind them the whole stair is listening.

effects.log: You say you understand, and stay on the ninth step all afternoon. The marshal salutes, and so, one by one, does everyone below.

choices.text: Ask why the steps are different

effects.log: You ask why the steps are different. The marshal has no answer, and says so, and is not forgiven for it by the stairs, but is by you.

choices.text: Come down and sit by the marshal

effects.log: You come down and sit by the marshal, on a step far too low. The Court talks about it for a decade, and the marshal never leaves your side.

events.text: The children of lesser houses are brought to play with you, and each has been told, plainly, to lose at every game. You discover this on the third day, when a small boy cries because he accidentally won. The games are all cloud-chess, and the board is the height of a pavilion.

effects.log: You win honestly, and say so loudly, and teach the losers how. By the end of the season three of them are dangerous, and all of them are friends.

choices.text: Lose on purpose, and make a show

effects.log: You lose on purpose, and make a show of it. They are relieved, and you are bored, and learn how thin a crowd's kindness is.

choices.text: Change the rules so nobody can lose

effects.log: You change the rules so nobody can lose. The tutors call it a heresy of governance and quietly adopt it for the ministries.

events.text: You slip out of the palace of cloud at dusk, which has never been done, and find the lower stairs full of immortals with no names on their sleeves, carrying water. One of them hands you a bucket without looking, assuming you are staff. The bucket is heavier than anything in your life so far.

effects.log: You carry it to the top, with both arms shaking. Nobody thanks you, and you have never been so pleased with a day.
You say who you are. The bucket is taken back with a bow so sudden that half the water goes over your shoes.
You ask where the water goes. A tired woman tells you, and for the first time the cloud-palace seems like a place that someone has to keep running.

events.text: At your first seat in the first row of the Jade Court, you are given a cushion of silver cloud and a rank you did not earn. The ministers speak to your hands, not your face. When your line is mentioned, everybody who loves it looks pleased and everybody who does not looks at their sleeves.

effects.log: You sit still and listen to everything, with a face so blank it earns a reputation for depth. You are mostly counting sleeves.
You answer a minister's question in a clear young voice. It is the wrong question, and the right answer, and the Court takes note.
You ask, politely, for a plainer cushion. It takes a week of memoranda, and it is granted, and the ministers cannot decide whether you are humble or dangerous.

events.text: Two tutors compete for you. One flatters, and everything you do is precedent; the other tells you, without softening, what you got wrong. The flatterer has the better tea. The honest one has the better manuscripts, and has quietly been taking notes on you for years, in case you ever ask what they were for.

effects.log: You keep the flatterer, and it is a pleasant decade. The mistakes pile up unseen, like snow on a roof, and one day you hear them fall.
You keep the honest tutor. It stings daily, and you grow, and your enemies find you harder to read than they hoped.

choices.text: Keep both, and listen to each

effects.log: You keep both, and learn to hear what each is selling. It is the most useful skill of your first three hundred years.

events.text: A match is proposed for you. Not a marriage yet, merely a betrothal of houses, with a young immortal of the Nine Clouds Palace whom you have met twice. The terms are generous. The young immortal looks as though they have also not been asked, and are waiting to learn if you will say something first.

effects.log: You accept for the line. The terms hold, the houses prosper, and the young immortal writes to you every year with careful, honest, unhurried courtesy.
You refuse, and say why, to the young immortal first. It is awkward, and kind, and both houses are offended exactly equally, which is a kind of fairness.

choices.text: Ask for a hundred years first

effects.log: You ask for a hundred years before any answer. The Court is scandalised and has to agree, because it has no rule against it.

events.text: The Ministries offer you a seat in a bureau of your own, which has never had an occupant under three thousand years. The post is small and the staff are old. They watch to see whether you will treat it as a toy or a duty, and the clerk of the bureau has already written both versions of the report.

choices.text: Take it, and work in it properly

effects.log: You take it, and work in it properly, from the first morning. By the end of the decade the bureau has never run so well, and the old staff have never looked so wary.

choices.text: Take it, and let the staff run it

effects.log: You take it, and let the staff run it. They do, wonderfully, and you learn how much of the Court is run by people you never see.
You refuse it as unearned. The Court is shocked, and then, slowly, a little impressed, and the post goes to a clerk who deserved it.

events.text: The heir of another first-row house has been your rival since the nursery clouds. Today they bow to you correctly, to the exact depth, and smile. Everything about it is perfect. It is the sort of courtesy that is practised in a mirror, and you recognise the mirror, because you have one too.

effects.log: You bow back, perfectly, to the exact depth. Nothing is said, and the whole Court sees a war declared by two people being very polite.
You ask them to tea, alone, with no one to see. It is stiff for an hour, and then not, and you both leave unwilling to be quite as perfect again.

choices.text: Outdo them at the next banquet

effects.log: You outdo them at the next banquet, in every detail. It costs a fortune in stones and a little in friendship, and you win.

events.text: A clerk of the Star Sea Pavilion sells you, for a modest price, a reading of your line from the stars. It is not flattering. The stars say your house has been living on the credit of an old victory, and that the credit is due in your lifetime. The clerk bows and does not ask for a refund.

effects.log: You pay for a second reading, and a third, until you are sure. The stars agree, wearily, each time. At least you can plan.

choices.text: Tell the head of your line

effects.log: You carry the reading to the head of your line, who reads it twice and burns it, and then, that night, quietly doubles the house's reserves.
You tell no one, and prepare. It is a lonely sort of work, and you are better at your line than anyone who simply inherited it.

events.text: Four powers send you gifts in one season: the Jade Void Sect a sword that has never been drawn, the Nine Clouds Palace an elixir with a name that cannot be said aloud, the Star Sea Pavilion a calendar of lucky days, the Ministries an appointment. Each gift is a hand held out. Each wants the same thing, which is your name beside theirs.

effects.log: You accept the sword, and hang it where it can be seen. The Jade Void Sect is delighted, and the others take notes on what that means.
You accept the appointment, and with it a quiet, long obligation to the Ministries. The sword and the elixir are returned politely, with notes.
You return all four with thanks and a perfectly equal letter. The Court has not seen anyone so careful in an age, and that, too, is a position.

events.text: The palace of cloud has weathered. The nurse who raised you has gone, and the second tutor, and the cook who knew how you took your tea. A portrait of you as a child hangs in the east hall, and strangers ask who it is. Your line has gone on, as lines do, and you have become its old part.

choices.text: Sit in the east hall a while

effects.log: You sit in the east hall with the portrait and a pot of tea. The child looks very sure, and you wish them well, and the tea goes cold.
You have the portrait taken down. It is a clean, brisk decision, and it hurts for exactly as long as you expected.

choices.text: Teach the strangers who it was

effects.log: You teach the strangers who it was, and by the end the east hall has an audience of young immortals asking what the first century was like.

events.text: A new child of your house is born, and the first row shifts one cushion to make room. You are now the old relative at the top of the hall, who is brought out on occasions to say something remembered. The infant is carried past you in a bundle of cloud and stares at you with the furious clarity of the very young.

effects.log: You hold the child, to the horror of nine attendants. The child grips your sleeve, and the attendants do not dare say a word.
You bless the child formally, as the old forms require. The Court is pleased, and you are glad when it is over.

choices.text: Tell the child the family secret

effects.log: You lean in and tell the child one true thing about the line, quietly, that no tutor will. The child will not remember. You will.

events.text: From the high stair you hear a tutor, the grandchild of your own, teaching the heir your own childhood lessons, word for word. The heir gets the ninth step wrong. The tutor corrects them, gently, and for a moment you are standing at the foot again, a very small thing, being told never to stand lower.

choices.text: Climb up and correct the tutor

effects.log: You climb up and correct the tutor on a point of precedence. It is a silly mistake, and everyone is very grateful, and you feel your age.
You leave them to it. The lesson is the same, and so is the stair, and that, you decide, is a comfort.

choices.text: Teach the heir a different lesson

effects.log: You find the heir that evening and teach them the lesson that was not in the book: how to stand on any step. They never forget it.

events.text: A young faction of the Court proposes reforming the precedence of the stairs, so that rank is earned rather than born. They come to you first, as the oldest holder of an inherited step, to see if you will oppose them. The stairs are very quiet. A very old marshal pretends to study the cloud.

effects.log: You support the reform, loudly, from your inherited step. Half the Court never forgives you, and the other half builds a better stair.
You oppose it, in the old form, with grace. The reform is delayed a century, and you are admired and slightly pitied for it.

choices.text: Offer to give up your own step

effects.log: You offer to give up your own step first, publicly, as proof. It is the most expensive and the most imitated thing you have ever done.

events.text: The head of your line grows weary, and the first row looks at you. The seat is yours to claim, if you speak. It is a great house, and a great weight, and a long, long future of other people's petitions. You can feel the whole stair waiting for you to say a word, or the lack of one.

effects.log: You claim the seat. The first row rises, all at once, with a sound like wind in jade. You take the cushion that was kept for you, and it is heavier than it looked.

choices.text: Renounce it, for your own road

effects.log: You renounce the seat. It is a quiet sentence, said once. The first row sits down again, and does not know where to look.

events.text: A cousin of your line has been named as the likelier successor, and does not know yet that you have been asked. They are decent, and tired, and would hold the seat well enough. The old marshal puts the question to you in private: the line, or the road? Both are open. Only one will be open tomorrow.

effects.log: You claim the line, and tell the cousin first, in person. They are relieved, and a little hurt, and write a very kind letter afterwards.
You back the cousin and renounce your claim. They cry, once, in the garden of clouds, and you are not sure which of you has been spared.

events.text: The Court asks for your answer before the Mid-Autumn feast. The Ministries want an heir. The Nine Clouds Palace wants a patron. The Jade Void Sect wants a sword on the throne. Nobody has asked what you want, and you realise, with a small cold shock, that you have never been asked in your life.

choices.text: Take the seat, and make it yours

effects.log: You take the seat, and make it yours: new rules, the old stairs, a window in the north hall. It is not what anyone wanted, and everyone comes round.
You walk away from the seat before the feast, and arrive at it as a guest. The cushion stays empty a year, then is filled, and the world carries on.

choices.text: Ask for ten more years to decide

effects.log: You ask for ten more years. The Court grants it, with an air of having been dreading the request, and nothing else changes.

events.text: An old tutor comes to your door at dusk, with a letter sealed in your line's silver. It says the seat is yours, and that your line has chosen. It says it will honour the other answer too, if you give it. It is signed by the very person you disliked most as a child, and who was, you now see, right.

choices.text: Accept the letter and the seat

effects.log: You accept the letter and the seat. The signer smiles, the way one smiles at a wall that has finally been mended.
You return the letter with your thanks, and renounce. The signer bows, and in the bow is a respect you never earned as a child.

events.text: You are born between two thrones, and neither of the gods who sit on them is looking at the other. The nursery is a room that rains softly when you cry, and thunders when you laugh, which is considered promising. Prayers drift in at the window like moths. A servant of the Silent Hall writes your first word in the Book of Fates, and then, quietly, rubs it out.

effects.log: You laugh, and the room thunders, and a distant worshipper somewhere looks up from a field and takes it for a good omen.
You reach for the prayers as they drift past and catch a few. One of them is a child's, asking for a pony. You do not know what a pony is yet, but you keep it.
You cry until someone comes. A very old god sits by the cot for an hour and says nothing. It is, you will learn, the greatest honour a thrones-child can have.

events.text: The first thing a child of the thrones learns is to be seen but not stared at. The gods of the Will of Heaven rule by being looked at; the gods of the Silent Hall by being remembered; the Green Assembly by having always been there; the Throne of Storms by being loud. You are taught the four and told to belong to none of them yet.

effects.log: You practise being seen, in the great glass, with a straight back. By evening you can fill a room with nothing but standing still, and it gives you a headache.
You practise being remembered, with small and exact kindnesses. A scullery god you thanked three weeks ago still tells the story.
You practise being loud, in a storm-room. It shakes a shelf of ancestors, and you are not allowed back for a decade.

events.text: Gods' children are brought to play with you, each one scrubbed and rehearsed. They bow at the right depth. They laugh at the right time. One of them, the smallest, a godling of ditches, forgets and kicks you in the shin instead. It is the first honest thing anyone has done to you.

effects.log: You kick back, with all the force of a god's nursery, and the two of you are inseparable for a hundred years. The tutors despair.
You laugh, and ask their name, which nobody has asked them in an age. They tell you, and it is a very good name, and you keep it.
You call a tutor, and the godling is taken away, red and silent. You will remember the silence for a very long time.

events.text: On the night of the great festival, you are allowed up to the balcony of the thrones and shown the worshippers: a river of lamps, all the way down. They are praying to the gods who sit beside you. They do not know you exist. A hundred thousand people have just asked for something, and your parent, beside you, yawns.

choices.text: Ask what they are asking for

effects.log: You ask what they are asking for. Your parent looks at you strangely and tells you. It is mostly rain, and a little love, and a great deal of bread.

choices.text: Throw a spark down to them

effects.log: You throw down a spark, a child's trick. A village far below has an unaccountably good harvest, and the thrones argue for a year about why.
You say nothing, and remember every lamp. Years later you will see a lamp in a dark room, and know exactly what it was asking.

events.text: At the thrones' feast, you are seated in the middle of the table. It is a place of terrible safety, equidistant from every god who might love you and every god who might use you. A senior god of the Green Assembly, ancient as soil, leans over and tells you that the middle seat is the loneliest one, and passes the salt.

choices.text: Move to the end of the table

effects.log: You move to the end of the table, among the young. The elders let you, with raised eyebrows, and the table is livelier for it.
You stay, and watch everyone. By the end of the feast you know exactly who is afraid of whom, and you have not said a word.

choices.text: Ask the old god about soil

effects.log: You ask the old god about soil. They talk until the candles go out. It is the best conversation in a thousand years, and they remember it.

events.text: Your divine tutor is a god of dreams, who teaches by making you sleep. You wake from each lesson knowing the thing and unable to say how. Today the lesson was in the form of your own childhood, played back with the colours wrong, and you wake angry, because someone in it was kind to you, and you cannot tell if they were real.

choices.text: Ask the tutor who it was

effects.log: You ask. The tutor, for once, does not answer with a riddle, and says the kind one was a servant, long since gone to the Silent Hall. You go and find their name.

choices.text: Refuse to sleep for a decade

effects.log: You refuse to sleep for a decade. It is a petulant gesture and the tutor admires it so much that they let you win the argument.
You ask to dream it again, slowly. The second time, the colours are right, and the servant looks at you, and says your name.

events.text: A suitor from another pantheon asks for your hand in the name of a peace, which is a courtesy. The old gods smile and speak about alliances. You have met the suitor twice, and once they were kind to a beetle. The treaty would take four hundred years to negotiate. You could stall it for four thousand.

effects.log: You accept, for the peace, and the thrones breathe out. The suitor writes you a letter about the beetle, and it is the kindest thing in the treaty.
You refuse, openly, in front of both pantheons. The old gods are furious and the suitor, to everyone's surprise, applauds.

choices.text: Stall the treaty for an age

effects.log: You stall the treaty for an age, with a long series of reasonable objections. By the end of it the peace has made itself.

events.text: A seat is held for you in the Heavenly Court of the gods, as a courtesy of birth: an honorary rank, with a robe, and a door that opens when you approach. The gods who earned theirs through ten thousand years of service watch you walk through it. Nobody is rude. It is just that the doors seem a little too eager.

choices.text: Use the seat as it was meant

effects.log: You use the seat as it was meant, and speak when asked, and are quietly good at it. The doors, over time, stop looking eager and begin to look respectful.

choices.text: Ask to start from the lowest rank

effects.log: You ask to start from the lowest rank. The Court refuses, three times, then lets you, and you spend a century filing prayers beside a god of broom closets.

choices.text: Leave the seat empty on purpose

effects.log: You leave the seat empty on purpose, and attend only when asked. The seat becomes a legend, and your absence a kind of power.

events.text: A rival godling of your age, born to another thrones' line, challenges you to a contest of omens: whose sign will the mortals notice first? You both go down, each in disguise, to a town of fishers, and arrange your signs. Theirs is a splendid rainbow. Yours, by accident, is a rainstorm that saves a drought-stricken field.

effects.log: You claim the field's victory, and the rival bows grudgingly. They will be a lifelong rival, and an honest one.
You concede that the rainbow was lovelier. The fishers keep it in a song for a thousand years, and your rival never forgets the generosity.

choices.text: Ask what the fishers actually wanted

effects.log: You ask the fishers what they wanted. It was neither. It was news of a lost boat, and the two of you spend the night finding it.

events.text: In the Book of Fates, you find your own page. It is lightly written, mostly in pencil, as if the scribes were not sure. A line near the bottom reads: will be asked to choose. The ink is dry, and not yours. A scribe, passing, sees what you are reading and blanches, and then does the decent thing and pretends to be blind.

choices.text: Read the page to the end

effects.log: You read the page to the end. There is not much, and you keep every word, and the pencil lines seem somehow like an offer.
You rub out the last line, with your thumb. It comes back in the morning, in the same pencil, with a tiny smudge where you were.

choices.text: Add a line of your own

effects.log: You add a line of your own, in ink, small. The scribes do not notice for a century, and then spend another trying to work out what it means.

events.text: A famine of faith strikes the low country, and the offerings to your birth-line thin to a trickle. The elders of the thrones meet in a cold hall to decide whether to cut the worship of the smaller domains to feed their own. They have invited you, as a courtesy of birth, to sit and not speak. You are old enough to know that what you do here will be remembered.

effects.log: You speak against the cut, though you were asked not to. The hall is cold with offence, and the cut is halved, and a hundred small gods keep their lamps lit through the lean years.

choices.text: Keep to the courtesy and listen

effects.log: You keep to the courtesy and listen. The cut goes through. You carry the sound of it with you for ages, and learn what silence costs.

choices.text: Offer a share of your own offerings

effects.log: You offer a share of your own offerings to the smaller domains. It is small, and public, and the thrones are embarrassed into matching it.

events.text: The thrones of your birth have aged, in the way gods do, which means the lamps are dimmer, the incense thicker, the servants more devoted. They ask you to dine. They ask nothing else. Across the table a throne that once frightened you is cutting its meat very small. It turns out that nothing was ever required of you but to come.

effects.log: You come to dinner every year, from then on. It is not a great deal. It is, you gather, everything.
You say what you never said, in three plain sentences, over the soup. The throne puts down its knife, and nods, and neither of you speaks for an hour.
You make it a formal visit, with gifts, and exactly the right words. It is a good visit. It is not the one anyone needed.

events.text: A newly-made god, young as dawn, is shown the thrones and the Halls by a nervous attendant, and stops in front of you to ask who you are. The attendant coughs. You say your name, and the young god has never heard it. It is, you realise, the first time in thousands of years you have been simply introduced.

effects.log: You let them stay ignorant for the whole afternoon, and take them to the best places. They remember you not as a throne's child, but as a friend.
You tell them your whole name, with all its titles. They do their best to look impressed, and it is touching.

choices.text: Ask them what they are for

effects.log: You ask the young god what they are for. They think about it for an hour. The answer is the best thing you hear all century.

events.text: Pantheons change. A throne once the greatest is whispered about, another rises, a hall is renamed, and your birth-line, which was once sat above all, now gets a politely lowered voice. You are old enough to be asked, by a young faction, to say what the line was like in its glory. They want it for a song.

effects.log: You tell the glorious version. The song is stirring, and wrong in all the right ways, and the line is grateful for it.
You tell the true version, small meannesses and all. The song is shorter, and better, and the line is angry for a century and then proud.

choices.text: Decline to tell it at all

effects.log: You decline to tell it at all. The song is written without you, and gets a good many things wrong, and you let it.

events.text: A mortal prays to you by name, your throne-child name, the one you were called before you had a domain. They could not know it. It must have been told by a servant, a thousand years ago, to somebody's grandmother. The prayer is for something small. You sit with it for a night, and nobody asks you to answer.

effects.log: You answer the prayer, discreetly. A mortal, far below, finds a lost ring, and does not wonder how, and tells nobody.
You keep the prayer, unanswered, in a small box. It is a strange sort of treasure, and sometimes you open it.
You find out who told them. It was a scullery servant, long ago, who was fond of you, and you go to the Silent Hall to say thank you.

events.text: A throne of your line is to be vacated. The old god who sat on it is ready to be remembered rather than worshipped, and has called the line to the hall of names. Everyone looks at you. It would be yours to take: the throne, the offerings, the weather in your name. The old god waits, with a face of terrible patience.

effects.log: You take the throne. The hall sings your name, once, in the old tongue, and prayers begin to arrive for you that were kept waiting for centuries.
You decline the throne. The old god bows to you, as to an equal, and the hall hums in a way that is partly grief and partly something older.

events.text: Your birth-line's elder tells you, without preamble, that the line needs a god it can see. The throne has been empty for a century and the offerings have started to go elsewhere. They do not ask you to take it. They only say that if you wish to, the way is open, and that if you do not, they will not be angry, and will be very tired.

effects.log: You sit on the empty throne. It is cold, and then it is not. Over the following decade the offerings return, one cup at a time.
You let the line choose another. The elder nods, as if relieved to hear the answer said aloud, and begins, at once, to look for someone good.

events.text: Two parties in the thrones' hall want two things. One wants you to take your line's seat, and carry on its custom. The other says that a child of the thrones has always been kept to the family seat, and it is time one made a name elsewhere. Neither will say what they will do if you disagree. You can tell that both mean it.

effects.log: You take the line's seat, and the first party throws a feast. The second sends a quiet note of support, which is worth more.

choices.text: Go and make a name elsewhere

effects.log: You go and make a name elsewhere. The first party never forgives you, and the second visits, every age, with a bottle.

choices.text: Ask for a century to think

effects.log: You ask for a century to think. The hall grants it with a sigh, and both parties return, the same, a hundred years later.

events.text: On the day of the naming, your birth-line's old servant, who has seen five of the line sit and fall, brings you the seat's cushion. They do not say what to do with it. They say only that it has been brushed, every morning, for two hundred years, in case. It is very clean. It is the best argument anyone makes.

choices.text: Take the cushion and the seat

effects.log: You take the cushion and the seat. The servant weeps without noise, and is the first to kneel.
You give the cushion back, kindly, and thank the servant for the brushing. They bow so low it is a kind of answer, and you hear the weeping later.

events.text: You are born in the palace of {b3_kingdom}, a child of its royal house, with a nurse for every hour of the day and a cradle carved from a single river-oak. The steward posts a notice at the gate. The cooks send up honey-cakes shaped like crowns, which you are too young to eat. Bells ring across the town, and at the temples they say a small prayer to the Maker.

effects.log: You grab the nearest honey-cake, crown and all. The cooks later insist it was an omen, and make them every year in that exact shape.
You stare at the temple bells until they stop. A nurse says you listen like an old person, and you do.

choices.text: Fall asleep in the middle of it

effects.log: You fall asleep in the middle of the ceremony. It is considered a sign of a calm temper, and is mentioned in your favour for years.

events.text: At six you are given a tutor, a tall dry woman who has taught three generations of the house and does not intend to be impressed. She teaches you the names of the rivers of {b3_kingdom} and the order in which the nobles must be greeted. You learn the rivers at once. The nobles, you decide, can wait.

effects.log: You learn all the rivers first, and draw them on the schoolroom floor. The tutor, to her own surprise, smiles.

choices.text: Ask why the nobles come first

effects.log: You ask why the nobles come first. The tutor is silent for a long moment and then tells you the truth, which is that nobody remembers.

choices.text: Memorise the nobles to please her

effects.log: You memorise the nobles to please her. By the end of the week you know every cousin, and they all say you are a pleasant child.

events.text: You find a door in the palace that no one has opened, behind a tapestry of the kingdom's founding. Inside is a small round room full of toys: wooden soldiers, a spinning-top, a broken boat. They belonged to a child of the house long ago, and have not been touched. Dust lies on them like fur.

choices.text: Take the boat to be mended

effects.log: You take the boat to be mended and sail it in the fountain. The steward looks very hard at you, and then at the door, and says nothing.

choices.text: Tell the steward about the room

effects.log: You tell the steward about the room. The steward goes pale and sits down. The room, it turns out, was sealed for grief.
You keep it a secret, and go back often. It is the only place in the palace where nobody is watching, and you are very careful with it.

events.text: On a feast day, the royal house of {b3_kingdom} rides through the town, and you are allowed on a pony beside the cart. The people line the road and cheer. You have never seen so many faces. One girl in the crowd holds up a loaf of bread as if offering it to you, and a guard steps in front, and the girl lowers it, embarrassed.

choices.text: Ask the guard to let her through

effects.log: You ask the guard to let her through. She gives you the loaf, and it is still warm, and the crowd cheers louder than for the cart.
You wave to the whole road, with great seriousness. You are told afterwards that it was a perfect royal wave and that you must never do it that way again.

choices.text: Look at the loaf, and keep riding

effects.log: You look at the loaf, and keep riding. You think about it for years, the bread and the lowered hand.

events.text: You are sent to the school of the royal house, where the children of nobles are taught the arts of rule. The first lesson is to stand when a superior enters. Your classmates stand for you. They stand a little too fast, and sit a little too carefully. A boy at the back, the son of a miller, scribbles something about the lesson and hides it.

choices.text: Ask to see what he wrote

effects.log: You ask to see what he wrote. It is a rude, accurate poem about the headmaster. You laugh, and so does he, and so, in time, does the headmaster.
You pretend not to notice. He is grateful, and quiet, and you gradually realise he is the only honest voice in the room.
You report him to the headmaster, because that is how rule is learned. You regret it before the day is out, and for a long time after.

events.text: A training master of the school of fighting arts in the hills has been engaged to teach you, and does not bow. He says that a blade does not care about the colour of your cloak, and puts a wooden sword in your hand. You hit the floor, the post, your own foot. He is patient and merciless in exactly the proportion that makes you better.

effects.log: You train until your hands blister, and then some. By the end of the year the master nods once, which is a speech.

choices.text: Ask to learn the footwork only

effects.log: You ask to learn only the footwork. He is surprised, then approving, and your body learns to be where the blade is not.
You complain to the steward. The master is replaced with a softer one, and you do not improve, and you feel it.

events.text: A match is hinted: a child of the royal house of a neighbouring kingdom, to be introduced at the harvest fair. The families have discussed it for a year without telling you. You are sixteen, and everyone around you has the studied calm of people hiding a plan. The child in question, when you meet, is eating a pear with deep attention, and looks up, startled, and says: I did not know either.

effects.log: You walk the fair with them, buying whatever sounds worst. It is the best day of the year, and the match is left, officially, open.
You speak plainly to the elders, and say you will decide for yourself. They are shocked, and then, one by one, relieved.
You accept for the peace. The border is quieter for it. The pear-eater writes to you every month, gently, as to someone who has been bought.

events.text: Your first post is a minor one: the keeping of the grain-houses on the river road. You inspect them in a plain coat, with a clerk. The first has a roof that leaks. The second has a thief in it, a thin boy with a sack. The third is empty, and the clerk tells you, without looking, that it has been empty for six years, and that the records say it is full.

effects.log: You report the empty house, to your own relative, with the figures. It is not welcome. It is, over the coming years, the thing that makes your name.

choices.text: Let the thief go, and fix the roof

effects.log: You let the thief go with a loaf, and fix the roof from your own purse. The clerk has a look on his face that is almost a smile.

choices.text: Ask the clerk what he knows

effects.log: You ask the clerk what he knows. It is a great deal, and he has been waiting years for someone to ask, and the kingdom's grain begins, quietly, to be counted.

events.text: A cousin of the royal house of {b3_kingdom} is accused of cheating at the river-boat races, and the accusation is true. Everyone knows. The cousin comes to you, with wet eyes, and asks you to say you were at the finish and saw nothing. It is a small lie. It would cost you a very little, and the cousin a very great deal to be without.

effects.log: You lie for the cousin. It works, and the cousin is grateful, and the debt of that small lie sits in the family like a stone in a boot.
You tell the truth, in the open. The cousin is disgraced for a season, and then, strangely, a better person, and writes you a letter of thanks.
You persuade the cousin to confess first. It takes the whole night. By dawn it is done, and the cousin is shaking and relieved, and the races are never the same.

events.text: At the great temple of the Maker, a priest asks the royal house to give thanks for the year. You stand in the first row, as always. Behind you, people are praying for rain, for a lost son, for a sick cow. You catch yourself listening to the prayers instead of your own. Something in the stone of the temple seems, for a moment, to be listening as well.

choices.text: Pray for the people behind you

effects.log: You pray for the people behind you, in your own words. When you open your eyes the priest is looking at you with a mild and thoughtful alarm.
You pray for your own house, as expected. It is a good prayer, and if anything listens, it is polite about it.
You stay silent and listen. You do not hear an answer. You hear, instead, the room, and how many people it is holding.

events.text: The palace you were born in is shabbier than you remembered. The stair where you learned to walk has a worn hollow, the nurses who sang to you have gone, and the tapestry of the kingdom's founding has been mended so often it is more patch than picture. A young steward asks, nervously, whether you would like it all renewed. It would cost a good deal.

effects.log: You renew it all, and the palace gleams. The young steward is proud. You walk through the new halls and cannot find the place where you learned to walk.
You mend only what is dangerous. The hollow in the stair stays. The steward is puzzled, and then, one afternoon, sees a child asleep in the worn place, and understands.

choices.text: Open the old rooms to the town

effects.log: You open the old rooms to the town for one day a year. The queues go round the hill, and the sealed door of toys is the one people love best.

events.text: A young child of the royal house is brought to you and told you are a very important relative. The child takes your hand with great solemnity, and asks if it is true that you used to be the one with the pony. You say it is true. The child nods, and says that the pony was in a story, and that they would like to hear what really happened.

effects.log: You tell them what really happened, which is much less grand and a great deal funnier. They laugh until they are sick, and write it down.
You tell them the grand story. They listen with their mouth open, and it is the right thing, and also not quite true, and you know it.

choices.text: Let them ride the old pony's saddle

effects.log: You find the old pony's saddle in the stable, and set the child on it. They are quiet a long time, and then ask for a pony of their own.

events.text: The harvest fair comes round, and the people of the town have set up a stall in honour of the royal house. It sells small clay figures of its members, all unflattering, all excellent. Yours has a very large nose and a very sad pony. The potter, an old woman, looks at you, and at the figure, and says the nose is right but she has never been sure about the pony.

effects.log: You buy the figure, and put it in your window. It is the only likeness of you anyone in the kingdom loves.
You tell the potter about the pony. She remakes the figure on the spot, and the pony is happy, and you are astonished at how much it matters to you.
You laugh, and order a hundred for the palace. The potter retires on the order, and the royal house of {b3_kingdom} is, thereafter, a little less stiff.

events.text: An old petitioner arrives at the palace gate and asks to speak to you by your childhood name, which almost no one now alive could know. They were once your nurse's assistant. They are very thin, and very straight, and have walked three days. They want nothing, they say. They only wanted to see whether the child who cried at midnight had grown into someone who listens.

choices.text: Have them to dinner at your table

effects.log: You have them to dinner at your table, in the plainest place. They say very little. At the end they thank you, and it is the only thanks you will remember.

choices.text: Ask what they remember of you

effects.log: You ask what they remember of you. It is a longer list than you expected, and a kinder one, and you write down every item.

choices.text: Give them a pension and a room

effects.log: You give them a pension and a room in the palace. They accept, with dignity, and are found a year later sitting in the nursery, quite content.

events.text: In the royal archive, you find the house's oldest ledger, and it is not a ledger of rule but of debts: grain borrowed from villages, labour borrowed from towns, an old forest taken without asking. The founders were thieves, politely. There is a line, in the margin, in a very old hand, asking that someone, someday, repay it.

choices.text: Begin to repay what is owed

effects.log: You begin to repay what is owed, slowly and in plain sight. It is controversial, and it is the most royal thing the house has done in a hundred years.
You publish the ledger. The people are quiet, and then angry, and then, eventually, a little proud that the house told them.
You seal the ledger again. It is the easy thing, and you know it, and the margin note stays in your mind like a burr.

events.text: The elder of the royal house of {b3_kingdom} is ill, and the council meets in the long room to name who will take the crown. All the eyes in it come to rest on you. It would be yours with a word, and the word would not be hard to say. The elder, from the couch, only looks at you and does not tell you what to answer.

effects.log: You claim the crown. The council rises, all together, with a sound of chairs, and for the first time you feel the whole weight of the kingdom settle on your shoulders like a coat.
You renounce the crown. The elder closes their eyes and smiles, as if you had passed a test, and the council tries to look as though it had expected this.

events.text: A cousin is plainly keen on the crown, and plainly unsuited. The council knows it. The cousin knows it, in some corner. They have come to you at night to say that they will step aside if you ask. It is a surprising offer, and a heavy one, because if you do not take it, you will have asked a friend to be a worse king for the kingdom.

choices.text: Take the crown, and make the cousin steward

effects.log: You take the crown, and make the cousin steward of the river road. It is a good place for them, and in time they are very good in it.

choices.text: Back the cousin, and step back

effects.log: You back the cousin and step back. It is a risk, and a kindness, and you become the first counsellor the cousin ever listens to.

events.text: The crown, in its box, is delivered to your door by a pair of nervous clerks. It is smaller than you thought, and plainer, and worn at the brow by the heads of eleven predecessors. A card says only: yours, if you want it. You turn it over. Inside the band someone has scratched, with a pin, a tiny word: sorry.

effects.log: You put it on. It fits as badly as everyone's, and the clerks sigh with relief, and the word presses against your forehead for the rest of your reign.

choices.text: Close the box and send it back

effects.log: You close the box and send it back, with a note. The clerks go pale, and then, outside, you hear one of them laugh, as if released.

choices.text: Ask for a year to learn the work

effects.log: You ask for a year to learn the work before deciding. The council grants it, and you spend it in the grain-houses, and come out knowing what you are being asked to rule.

events.text: A letter comes from the temple of the Maker: the high priest, unusually, says that there is no sign for the succession, and that anyone who claims one is lying. It says the crown is a human question. It adds, in the margin, that the priest has known you since you were small, and that either answer will be, in their experience, survivable.

effects.log: You claim the crown, plainly, in a public hall. The priest is the first to kneel, and gets up again with a hand on the wall.

choices.text: Renounce it, and tell the priest

effects.log: You renounce the crown, and tell the priest first. They hear it with the calm of a person who has prepared for either, and say the Maker never asked for kings.
